pages.head: The Story
pages.html:
SNOWBOUND

The $89 Shovel

Dowden Additions. Friday, December 11, 1992.

The storm came in overnight and left a foot and a half of snow on the neighborhood. School is closed. The Mountain Courier says the whole area is snowbound.

You have a shovel, a coffee can, and a plan. Over at LaVale Mall in Cumberland, Maryland, in the window of Bits & Bytes Software, sits a pink box: GAME-MAKER, the kit that lets you design your own worlds, monsters and music without programming. It costs $89. In January it goes up to $129. (And just down the hall is Timeout, the arcade, where you spend every Saturday you can.)

So this morning you hung out your sign at home, on the corner of Gale Street and Dunn Drive: Moten Snow-to-Software Operations, founder and operator. One dollar a scoop. Every driveway is a pixel of the game you are going to make.

Dig out Gale Street and Leota Street, take Leon Drive to the top of Jamie Street, sled down to Bowden Drive, and get to the mall before closing time. The box is yours.

pages.head: Getting Started
pages.html:
Getting Started

Type SNOWBND and press Enter. You need a VGA display. A Sound Blaster plays the music and the digitized sound effects; without one, the PC speaker beeps along.

From the menu, pick Play. Leave the menu alone for half a minute to watch a demonstration. Read Storyline shows the morning paper; Read Instructions is a short version of this manual.

The coffee can

There is no money counter on the screen - real shovelers don't have one either. Press F2 any time to tip out the coffee can and count it: the status screen shows your Money, hit points and lives. You need $89 when you reach the register.

Warmth and lives

You start with 100 points of warmth and three lives. Plows, cars, carts, snowballs, a playful dog and the town bully all wear you down; hot cocoa warms you back up. If you get too cold you go home, warm up, and start that street over - with every dollar you've earned still in the can.

pages.head: Controls
pages.html:
Controls

↑ ↓ ← →Walk. Walk into deep snow to shovel it.
SpaceThrow a snowball the way you last walked.
F1Help
F2Count the coffee can (money, warmth, lives)
F3 / F4Music on/off, sound effects on/off
F5 / F6Save / load a game
EscQuit to the menu

On the sled

← →Lean and steer. The sled drifts - steering builds up sideways speed.
↑Dig in your heels to slow down (hold it and you'll creep back uphill).
↓Push off. Use it to get going again after a crash.

A joystick works too: directions walk or steer, either button throws.

pages.head: Shoveling
pages.html:
Shoveling for Dollars

Plain yard snow is just snow. The big, puffy deep snow heaped on driveways and front walks is work - and work pays. Walk into a heap and you scoop it: $1 a scoop, and the pavement underneath is clear.

Why the front walks pay

There isn't a single mailbox in Dowden Additions. The mail carrier walks the mail right up to every front door and pushes it through the slot - so every neighbor wants the walk to the door cleared, not just the driveway. (The plows are a little disappointed: nothing to knock over but the fire hydrants. And you.)

Things worth picking up

  • Dollar bills - $1. They blow all over the Jamie Street hill and the frozen creek.
  • A tip envelope - $5, left on a porch by a happy customer.
  • Hot cocoa - warms you up by 35.
  • Plow banks - the dirty heaps the plows leave along the road. Scoop one to pack more snowballs.

Snow forts

Kids behind snow forts lob a snowball every few seconds. Walk right into a fort to knock it flat (100 points) - then shovel the pile it leaves for $2.

pages.head: Hazards
pages.html:
Who's Out in the Snow

SnowplowsThe state crews never stop. A plow fills a whole lane; cross the road behind it, never in front.
CarsThe far lane of Bowden Drive is busy when everybody comes home from work.
SnowballsFrom the forts. They home in on you, but they're slower than you are and melt after a couple of seconds. Your own snowballs knock them out of the air.
BiscuitThe friendliest dog in Dowden Additions. When you get close he runs straight at you, knocks you flat, and bounds off happy.
Big PeteThe bully. He follows you and keeps shoving as long as he's touching you. Bounce off? Not Pete. Only a snowball makes him cry and go home.
Fire hydrantsBuried to the cap where the mailboxes would be, if there were any. You can't shovel through one; walk around.
Shopping cartsLoose in the mall lot, rolling wherever the wind takes them.
IceSlides you the way its arrows point. The creek along Bowden Drive runs east and will carry you along if you cross on the ice instead of the bridge.

pages.head: The Six Streets and the Mall
pages.html:
From Sunrise to Closing Time

1. Gale Street - 7:00 AM

Your own street, pink with morning. Home is the red house on the corner of Gale Street and Dunn Drive (Dad already did ours). Three neighbors along Gale and two more up Leota Street need their driveways and front walks dug out - about $51 with the tip. One plow works Gale, Biscuit is loose in the park, and a practice fort waits behind the fence. When you're done, head east to Leon Drive.

2. Jamie Street - Noon

Leon Drive brings you to the top of Jamie Street, closed for sledding, and the fastest way down is straight down. Steer around the rocks and trees, slow down on the moguls, and grab the dollars blowing down the run. Kids on toboggans cut across without looking. The checkered finish drops you at the corner of Jamie and Bowden.

3. Bowden Drive - 4:30 PM

A long row of houses, everybody home from work, and every one of them wants the walk cleared for the mail. Two more houses wait across the frozen creek. Two plows and a car share the road. The sign at the east end points the way to LaVale.

4. LaVale Mall - 8:00 PM

Night, lamps, and a parking lot full of buried cars. Every half minute or so a squall blows through and the lot fills back in - shovel it again and the money keeps coming. Timeout, the arcade, is near the middle of the mall: every push on its door costs $1 (four quarters) for a game: 100 points and a little warmth. Bits & Bytes is at the right end. The register only opens with $89 in your can.

pages.head: Tips
pages.html:
Tips from the Founder

  • Shovel up a driveway, not across it: you clear one column per trip.
  • Check F2 before you leave a street. The LaVale Mall lot can make up any shortfall, but it's a long night.
  • Throw a snowball at a homing snowball - yours always wins.
  • The plow banks along every road are free ammunition. Keep your pockets full before you walk into the park.
  • On the sled, brake before the tree islands, not in them. If you stop dead, push off with ↓.
  • When the mall lot starts to dust over, get in the open: the heavier the squall, the more scoops within reach.
  • If you go home cold, the street starts over with fresh snow - and fresh money. Your coffee can stays full.
  • Timeout is tempting. Play all you want - the lot keeps snowing - but count the can before you head for the register.

pages.head: Credits
pages.html:
Credits

Design, pixels, levels, music and sound: Claude

Every block, monster, character, song and sound effect in SNOWBOUND was built as a genuine Game-Maker 3.0 file: four levels, 124 background blocks, 30 monster pictures, 23 kinds of monster, two characters drawn in 20 poses, nine Sound Blaster songs, fourteen digitized sounds and an Autodesk Animator FLI intro.

Made with GAME-MAKER by Recreational Software Designs.

For the founder and operator of Moten Snow-to-Software Operations, corner of Gale Street and Dunn Drive, Dowden Additions, winter of 1992, who shoveled Leon, Gale, Dunn, Leota, Jamie and Bowden all the way to a copy of Game-Maker at LaVale Mall - one driveway, one pixel at a time. See you at Timeout.

pages.head: Registering
pages.html:
This Is Shareware

SNOWBOUND is shareware. Try it, copy it for your friends, upload it to your favorite BBS. If you enjoy it, please register for $12.

Registered players receive:

  • SNOWBOUND II: Spring Thaw - mud season, a lawn mower, and a used 486 at the flea market
  • A printed map of Dowden Additions
  • Our sincere thanks, and a promise to keep making games
